```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(highway)
```

This package bundles the [Google Highway](https://github.com/google/highway) C++
library so that R packages can use fast, portable SIMD code through
`LinkingTo`. Every C++ listing below is for display purposes when the
vignette is built, whilst the R output shown comes from small functions
compiled into this package itself.

# 1. Why this package?

SIMD instructions (*single instruction, multiple data*) process several
numbers at once: e.g., one AVX2 instruction adds four doubles, one AVX-512
instruction adds eight. For computationally heavy code this can often give a 2
to 8 times speed-up over plain C/C++ loops.

There are various ways to write SIMD code: in assembly (rarely!); with compiler intrinsics (C or C++ functions that map directly to individual CPU instructions,
tying the code to one CPU family); or perhaps most commonly with a C or C++
library such as [`SIMDe`](https://github.com/simd-everywhere/simde),
[`EVE`](https://github.com/jfalcou/eve) or
[`std::experimental::simd`](https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/experimental/simd).
These libraries work across CPU families, but they do not support so-called
"runtime dispatch" ... in other words, the target instruction set must be chosen
at compile time.

However, CRAN builds Windows and macOS binary packages once, for every user's
machine, without CPU-specific compiler flags. Hence, the compiler can only
assume a baseline capability: typically SSE2 on x86-64 and NEON on arm64. Code
compiled with `-mavx2` would crash with "illegal instruction" on a CPU without
AVX2, and CRAN does not allow such flags anyway! So for R packages we need a
way for the instruction set to be chosen at **run time**.

With Google Highway, you write a C++ function (called a *kernel*) once using
the Highway SIMD operations. The function is then compiled separately for each
*target* (instruction set) without needing CPU-specific compiler flags (so no
CRAN issue), and at run time Highway automatically calls the best version that
the CPU supports.

On the machine that built this vignette:

```{r targets}
supported_targets()   # what this CPU can run, best first
compiled_targets()    # what this package's own kernels were compiled for
dispatched_target()   # what they actually use here
```

`EMU128` and `SCALAR` are portable fallbacks that need no SIMD instructions.

Other C and C++ libraries, such as
[`xsimd`](https://github.com/xtensor-stack/xsimd) and
[`libsimdpp`](https://github.com/p12tic/libsimdpp), also support runtime
dispatch, but using that dispatch in an R package is difficult because to the
best of the author's knowledge they generally require compiling separate source
files with CPU-specific compiler flags, which `R CMD check` reports as a
warning.

# 2. Quick start

**Step 1: set up the package.** In the root of your package, run
`highway::use_highway()`. For example, running it on a minimal package in a
temporary directory produces the following:

```{r quickstart}
pkg <- file.path(tempdir(), "mysimd")
dir.create(pkg)
writeLines(c("Package: mysimd", "Version: 0.0.1", "Title: My SIMD",
             "License: MIT"), file.path(pkg, "DESCRIPTION"))
use_highway(pkg)
```

The package now has `LinkingTo: highway` and these files in `src/`:

```{r quickstart-files}
cat(readLines(file.path(pkg, "DESCRIPTION")), sep = "\n")
list.files(file.path(pkg, "src"))
cat(readLines(file.path(pkg, "src", "Makevars")), sep = "\n")
cat(readLines(file.path(pkg, "src", "highway-impl.cpp")), sep = "\n")
```

```{r quickstart-cleanup, include = FALSE}
unlink(pkg, recursive = TRUE)
```

* `highway-impl.cpp` compiles Highway's small runtime (CPU detection, the
  chosen target, error handling) **once** for your package.
* `Makevars` and `Makevars.win` add `-I.` to `PKG_CPPFLAGS`, which runtime
  dispatch needs (section 4).
* `highway-kernels.cpp` and `highway-kernels.h` hold two example kernels
  (`add_doubles()` and `exp_doubles()`).

**Step 2: write a kernel**, or edit the examples (see sections 3 to 6 below for
full details).

**Step 3: call it from R.** For example, with the plain R C API, this involves
a single `.Call` entry point (see section 7 for Rcpp and cpp11 details):

```cpp
#define R_NO_REMAP
#include <Rinternals.h>
#include "highway-kernels.h"
#include "highway/r_guard.h"

extern "C" SEXP mysimd_exp(SEXP x) {
  const R_xlen_t n = Rf_xlength(x);
  SEXP out = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(REALSXP, n));
  const double* px = REAL(x);
  double* pout = REAL(out);
  HIGHWAY_R_BEGIN
    mysimd_hwy::exp_doubles(px, pout, static_cast<size_t>(n));
  HIGHWAY_R_END
  UNPROTECT(1);
  return out;
}
```

Register it as usual (for example with `tools::package_native_routine_registration_skeleton()`),
add `useDynLib(mysimd, .registration = TRUE)` to `NAMESPACE`, and wrap it:

```r
simd_exp <- function(x) .Call(mysimd_exp, as.double(x))
```

# 3. Your first kernel: static dispatch

A Highway kernel works on vectors described by a *tag*. `ScalableTag<double>`
means "a full vector of doubles for the current target"; `Lanes(d)` is how
many doubles that is (2 for SSE2 and NEON, 4 for AVX2, 8 for AVX-512).

```cpp
#include "hwy/highway.h"
namespace hn = hwy::HWY_NAMESPACE;

// out[i] = a[i] + b[i]
void add_doubles(const double* a, const double* b, double* out, size_t n) {
  const hn::ScalableTag<double> d;
  const size_t N = hn::Lanes(d);
  size_t i = 0;
  for (; i + N <= n; i += N) {                       // whole vectors
    const auto va = hn::LoadU(d, a + i);
    const auto vb = hn::LoadU(d, b + i);
    hn::StoreU(hn::Add(va, vb), d, out + i);
  }
  if (i < n) {                                       // the tail
    const size_t rem = n - i;
    hn::StoreN(hn::Add(hn::LoadN(d, a + i, rem), hn::LoadN(d, b + i, rem)),
               d, out + i, rem);
  }
}
```

Points to note:

* **Use unaligned loads and stores** (`LoadU`, `StoreU`). R allocates vectors
  with 8- or 16-byte alignment, not the 32 or 64 bytes AVX2 and AVX-512
  prefer ... the aligned `Load`/`Store` would fault, whereas on current CPUs
  unaligned access costs little.
* **Handle the tail.** `LoadN` loads the remaining `rem < N` elements and
  zero-fills the other lanes; `StoreN` writes only `rem` elements, so nothing
  past the end of the R vector is touched.
* Alternatively `hwy/contrib/algo/transform-inl.h` provides `Transform1()`
  and related functions, which handle the loop and the tail for you.

Code like this, compiled in a file that does not use `foreach_target.h`, uses
*static dispatch*: it is compiled once for the baseline target (on CRAN's
x86-64 binaries this is SSE2, giving 2 lanes of doubles rather than 4 or 8).
However, if static dispatch is sufficient, `highway-impl.cpp` is not
needed: delete it and add `-DHWY_HEADER_ONLY` to `PKG_CPPFLAGS` instead, so
that Highway's few non-inline functions are provided inline.

However, if you're using this package, it is probably because you want ...

# 4. Runtime dispatch

To use AVX2 and AVX-512 where available, compile the kernel for every target
and dispatch at run time. The full pattern (which `use_highway()` writes
into `highway-kernels.cpp`) is as follows:

```cpp
#include <stddef.h>
#include "highway-kernels.h"

// (1) Re-include this file once per target. The name is resolved against the
//     include path, not this file's directory: that is why src/Makevars
//     needs PKG_CPPFLAGS = -I.
#undef HWY_TARGET_INCLUDE
#define HWY_TARGET_INCLUDE "highway-kernels.cpp"
#include "hwy/foreach_target.h"  // must come before highway.h

#include "hwy/highway.h"

// (2) Per-target code goes between these markers, in HWY_NAMESPACE, which
//     expands to N_SSE2, N_AVX2, N_AVX3, N_NEON, ... in turn. The anonymous
//     namespace keeps the per-target copies private to this file.
HWY_BEFORE_NAMESPACE();
namespace mysimd_hwy {
namespace HWY_NAMESPACE {
namespace {
namespace hn = hwy::HWY_NAMESPACE;

void AddImpl(const double* HWY_RESTRICT a, const double* HWY_RESTRICT b,
             double* HWY_RESTRICT out, size_t n) {
  // ... the loop from section 3 ...
}

}  // namespace
}  // namespace HWY_NAMESPACE
}  // namespace mysimd_hwy
HWY_AFTER_NAMESPACE();

// (3) Code that must exist only once (not per target) goes in HWY_ONCE.
#if HWY_ONCE
namespace mysimd_hwy {

HWY_EXPORT(AddImpl);  // a table of AddImpl for every compiled target

void add_doubles(const double* a, const double* b, double* out, size_t n) {
  // (4) Calls the best AddImpl for this CPU. The first call detects the CPU;
  //     later calls are an indirect call through the table.
  HWY_DYNAMIC_DISPATCH(AddImpl)(a, b, out, n);
}

}  // namespace mysimd_hwy
#endif
```

In addition, `src/highway-impl.cpp` (and no other file) contains:

```cpp
#include "highway/impl.h"
```

`highway/impl.h` contains Highway's compiled runtime. Since R packages
cannot link against another package's shared library, each package compiles
its own copy; its symbols are hidden so that two packages using Highway in
the same R session cannot interfere with each other.

# 5. Transcendental functions

`hwy/contrib/math/math-inl.h` provides vectorised `Exp`, `Log`, `Sin`, `Cos`,
`Tanh`, `Atan2` and more, for `float` and `double`. Upstream documents their
accuracy and valid input range, for example (double precision):

| Function | Max error | Valid range |
|----------|-----------|-------------|
| `Exp`    | 1 ULP     | [-DBL_MAX, 706] |
| `Log`    | 4 ULP     | (0, DBL_MAX] |
| `Sin`, `Cos` | 3 ULP | [-39000, 39000] |

1 ULP is one unit in the last place (about 2.2e-16 relative error for
doubles). Base R's `exp()` and `log()` call the C library, which is usually
within 1 ULP too, so results may differ from base R in the last bit or two:

```{r accuracy}
x <- seq(-20, 20, length.out = 1e5)
max(abs(hwy_demo_exp(x) / exp(x) - 1))
max(abs(hwy_demo_log(x[x > 0]) / log(x[x > 0]) - 1), na.rm = TRUE)
```

**Outside the valid range, and for `NA`, `NaN` and `Inf`, Highway gives no
guarantees.** Note that in R `NA_real_` is a NaN with a special payload (the
low word is 1954), which is how R distinguishes `NA` from `NaN`. Hence, be aware
that SIMD arithmetic may return a NaN without that payload, essentially turning
an `NA` into `NaN`.

The demo kernels avoid this problem by checking each vector: if every lane is
an ordinary value in range, the SIMD path is used; otherwise that vector is
computed lane by lane like base R. Specifically, the scalar fallback calls
the C library while returning NaN inputs unchanged (R's own `exp()` does
this because on some CPUs, such as RISC-V, even the C library's `exp(NA)`
returns a NaN without the payload).

```cpp
const auto lo = hn::Set(d, -708.0), hi = hn::Set(d, 706.0);
const auto v = hn::LoadU(d, x + i);
// Comparisons with NaN (including NA) are false, so they fail this test.
if (hn::AllTrue(d, hn::And(hn::Ge(v, lo), hn::Le(v, hi)))) {
  hn::StoreU(hn::Exp(d, v), d, out + i);
} else {
  for (size_t j = i; j < i + N; ++j) {
    out[j] = std::isnan(x[j]) ? x[j] : std::exp(x[j]);
  }
}
```

```{r na-nan}
x <- c(1, NA, NaN, Inf, -Inf, 0, -0, 710, -750)
identical(hwy_demo_exp(x), exp(x))
is.na(hwy_demo_exp(x)) & !is.nan(hwy_demo_exp(x))   # NA stays NA
```

Since ordinary data rarely contains such values, the check costs little. If
you only need `NA`/`NaN` to remain unchanged, a mask is enough:
`hn::IfThenElse(hn::IsNaN(v), v, hn::Exp(d, v))` keeps the input lane, and
its payload, wherever the input is NaN.

# 6. Working with R types

**Doubles** (`REALSXP`) map directly onto `ScalableTag<double>`.

**Integers** (`INTSXP`) are 32-bit `int`, and `NA_integer_` is the smallest
`int` (`INT_MIN`), not a special bit pattern. So, SIMD integer arithmetic treats
it as an ordinary integer: `NA + 1` silently becomes `-2147483647`!! Therefore,
mask NA lanes explicitly, and widen before summing to avoid overflow:

```cpp
// Sum of an integer vector, skipping NA, accumulated in 64-bit integers.
double sum_int_na_rm(const int32_t* x, size_t n) {
  const hn::ScalableTag<int32_t> d32;
  const hn::Repartition<int64_t, decltype(d32)> d64;  // half as many lanes
  const size_t N = hn::Lanes(d32);
  const auto na = hn::Set(d32, std::numeric_limits<int32_t>::min());
  auto acc = hn::Zero(d64);
  size_t i = 0;
  for (; i + N <= n; i += N) {
    const auto v = hn::LoadU(d32, x + i);
    const auto clean = hn::IfThenZeroElse(hn::Eq(v, na), v);  // NA -> 0
    acc = hn::Add(acc, hn::SumsOf2(clean));  // adjacent pairs, as int64
  }
  int64_t total = hn::ReduceSum(d64, acc);
  for (; i < n; ++i) {
    if (x[i] != std::numeric_limits<int32_t>::min()) total += x[i];
  }
  return static_cast<double>(total);
}
```

**Logicals** (`LGLSXP`) are also stored as `int`: 0 for `FALSE`, 1 for
`TRUE`, `INT_MIN` for `NA`.

**When to stay scalar.** SIMD is most effective for long, contiguous vectors
of numbers with the same work per element. Keep scalar code for character
vectors and lists, irregular memory access (although Highway has gathers),
heavy data-dependent branching, very short vectors (a few dozen elements),
and places where the code is not a measured bottleneck.

# 7. Calling kernels from Rcpp, cpp11 and plain `.Call`

The kernels are plain C++ functions that take pointers and lengths, so they
work with any R interface. The only rule is that a C++ exception must not
escape into R. Highway's abort handler (which runs if Highway detects an
internal error) is set up to throw `highway::abort_error`, derived from
`std::runtime_error`, instead of terminating R.

**Rcpp** converts C++ exceptions to R errors automatically:

```cpp
#include <Rcpp.h>
#include "highway-kernels.h"

// [[Rcpp::export]]
Rcpp::NumericVector simd_exp(Rcpp::NumericVector x) {
  Rcpp::NumericVector out(x.size());
  mysimd_hwy::exp_doubles(x.begin(), out.begin(), x.size());
  return out;
}
```

**cpp11** does the same:

```cpp
#include <cpp11.hpp>
#include "highway-kernels.h"

[[cpp11::register]]
cpp11::writable::doubles simd_exp(cpp11::doubles x) {
  cpp11::writable::doubles out(x.size());
  mysimd_hwy::exp_doubles(REAL(x.data()), REAL(out.data()), x.size());
  return out;
}
```

**Plain `.Call`** can use the `HIGHWAY_R_BEGIN` / `HIGHWAY_R_END` macros from
`highway/r_guard.h`, as in section 2. They catch any C++ exception thrown
between them, copy its message to a buffer, leave the `try`/`catch` block
and only then call `Rf_error()`, because `Rf_error()` uses `longjmp`, which
must not jump out of a `catch` block (the exception would never be cleaned
up). Consequently,
allocate and protect R objects *before* `HIGHWAY_R_BEGIN`, declare any C++
objects with destructors *between* the macros, and do not call the R API
inside the block (where an R error would `longjmp` past them).

# 8. Using Highway from a package written in C

Highway is a C++ library, but a package whose code is in C can still use it:
the kernels live in one C++ file and are exposed through a plain C interface.
Call `use_highway(language = "c")` to set this up. The generated header,
`src/highway-kernels.h`, can be included from `.c` files:

```c
#include "highway/c_status.h"

int mysimd_hwy_add(const double* a, const double* b, double* out, size_t n,
                   char* err, size_t err_len);
int mysimd_hwy_exp(const double* x, double* out, size_t n,
                   char* err, size_t err_len);
```

The C++ side then wraps each kernel in `highway::c_guard()`:

```cpp
extern "C" int mysimd_hwy_exp(const double* x, double* out, size_t n,
                              char* err, size_t err_len) {
  return highway::c_guard([&] {
    using namespace mysimd_hwy;
    HWY_DYNAMIC_DISPATCH(ExpImpl)(x, out, n);
  }, err, err_len);
}
```

Your C code then checks the status on R's main thread:

```c
SEXP c_exp(SEXP x) {
  R_xlen_t n = XLENGTH(x);
  SEXP out = PROTECT(Rf_allocVector(REALSXP, n));
  char err[256];
  int status = mysimd_hwy_exp(REAL(x), REAL(out), (size_t) n, err, sizeof err);
  UNPROTECT(1);
  if (status != HIGHWAY_STATUS_OK) Rf_error("SIMD kernel failed: %s", err);
  return out;
}
```

This boundary is needed because C cannot catch C++ exceptions, and an
exception that reaches a C frame terminates the whole R process. Raw
pointers, lengths and an integer status code are the common interface across
both languages, and R compiles and links packages that mix `.c` and `.cpp`
files without further settings.

# 9. Calling kernels from other threads and through C interfaces

Highway kernels can run on any thread (worker threads your package creates,
or threads owned by another native library that calls your code back),
subject to the following rules:

* **No R API calls inside kernels.** The R API may only be used on R's main
  thread. Copy what you need out of R objects first and pass pointers.
* **Exceptions must not cross a thread boundary or a C interface.** Catch
  them with `highway::c_guard()` inside the thread function or callback and
  pass the status back.
* **Keep per-call state on the stack or in caller-owned buffers.** Kernels
  should not use global mutable state.
* Highway's own state is safe: the first dispatch may happen on several
  threads at once. To move the one-time CPU detection out of the first call,
  call `highway::warm_up()` from `highway/runtime.h` in your package's
  `R_init_<pkg>()`.
* Custom handlers set with `hwy::SetAbortFunc()` or `hwy::SetWarnFunc()` may
  run on any thread, so they must be thread-safe and must not call the R
  API. (The default warning handler does nothing; the default abort handler
  throws `highway::abort_error`.)

The following splits an array into chunks, one per thread, with SIMD inside
each chunk:

```cpp
#include <thread>
#include <vector>
#include "highway/c_guard.h"

// Returns HIGHWAY_STATUS_OK or the first error status.
int exp_parallel(const double* x, double* out, size_t n, int nthreads) {
  std::vector<int> status(nthreads, HIGHWAY_STATUS_OK);
  std::vector<std::thread> pool;
  const size_t chunk = (n + nthreads - 1) / nthreads;
  for (int t = 0; t < nthreads; ++t) {
    pool.emplace_back([&, t] {
      const size_t begin = t * chunk;
      const size_t end = begin + chunk < n ? begin + chunk : n;
      status[t] = highway::c_guard([&] {
        if (begin < end) mysimd_hwy::exp_doubles(x + begin, out + begin, end - begin);
      });
    });
  }
  for (auto& th : pool) th.join();
  for (int s : status) if (s != HIGHWAY_STATUS_OK) return s;
  return HIGHWAY_STATUS_OK;
}
```

Do not create more threads than the user expects. CRAN checks allow at most
two, and R sessions often run inside parallel jobs already. Let the user
choose the number (an argument or an option), and default to a small number.

# 10. Checking which target ran, and benchmarking

To see what your own kernels use, export a tiny dispatched function returning
`HWY_TARGET` (this package's `dispatched_target()` works that way) and turn
it into a name with `hwy::TargetName()`:

```cpp
int64_t TargetImpl() { return HWY_TARGET; }  // per target, in HWY_NAMESPACE
// ... in HWY_ONCE:
HWY_EXPORT(TargetImpl);
const char* my_target() { return hwy::TargetName(HWY_DYNAMIC_DISPATCH(TargetImpl)()); }
```

To compare against base R:

```r
x <- runif(1e6, -10, 10)
bench::mark(exp(x), hwy_demo_exp(x), check = FALSE)
```

Results on one machine (Apple M1, macOS, R 4.6.2, dispatched target `NEON`,
vectors of one million doubles; median times):

| Operation | Base R | Highway demo | Speed-up |
|-----------|-------:|-------------:|---------:|
| `exp()`   | 7.9 ms | 2.2 ms | 3.7x |
| `log()`   | 3.4 ms | 1.7 ms | 2.0x |
| `sum()`   | 1.7 ms | 0.19 ms | 9x |

Note that R's `sum()` accumulates in extended precision where available,
which accounts for part of the difference. Larger gains may be expected with
AVX2 and AVX-512 on x86-64, though you should measure on your own workload.

# 11. Submitting your package to CRAN

* **No `-m` flags.** Never add `-mavx2`, `-march=native` or similar to
  `Makevars`; runtime dispatch makes them unnecessary, and CRAN rejects them.
* **Install time.** Dynamic dispatch compiles each kernel once per target.
  Highway's default is up to 9 targets on x86-64. Define
  `HIGHWAY_TARGETS_LEAN` before the first Highway include of a kernel file
  (the `use_highway()` template does) to compile SSE2, SSE4, AVX2 and AVX3 on
  x86-64 and NEON, SVE and SVE2 on arm64 only. For full control, define
  `HWY_DISABLED_TARGETS` yourself, for example
  `#define HWY_DISABLED_TARGETS (HWY_SSSE3 | HWY_AVX3_SPR)`.
* **Do not call `abort()`, `exit()` or `printf()`, or write to `stderr`,** in
  your own code; R CMD check looks for these symbols. Highway's own uses have
  been patched out of the bundled copy.
* **Authors and copyright.** CRAN's practice for header packages used through
  `LinkingTo` (for example BH and RcppEigen) is that packages using them do
  *not* list the authors of the bundled library in `Authors@R`: the
  third-party sources are part of the header package, not of yours. Your
  package's compiled code does, however, contain compiled Highway code, and
  Highway is distributed under the BSD 3-Clause License, which asks that
  binary redistributions reproduce its copyright notice. A one-line note in
  your package's documentation (for example in `inst/COPYRIGHTS`: "Compiled
  code includes the 'Highway' library, Copyright Google LLC and other Highway
  authors, BSD 3-Clause License; see the 'highway' package") is a simple way
  to meet that requirement. If you copy Highway's headers into your own
  package instead of using `LinkingTo`, list the copyright holders as `cph`
  (see `system.file("COPYRIGHTS", package = "highway")`). **Note:** this is a
  summary of common practice and strictly not legal advice!!
* **C++ standard.** Highway needs C++17 or later, which is R's default from R
  4.4.0. Do not set `CXX_STD` to an older standard.
* **Win-builder testing.** Windows uses GCC (Rtools) with its own ABI for
  vector registers; run `devtools::check_win_devel()` and check that your
  tests exercise the dispatched kernels with vector lengths that are not a
  multiple of the vector size.

# 12. Troubleshooting

* **Long compile times.** Use `HIGHWAY_TARGETS_LEAN` (section 11), keep
  kernels in few files, and use [ccache](https://ccache.dev) on your own
  machine (for example `CXX = ccache g++` in your personal `~/.R/Makevars`,
  never in the package).
* **"illegal instruction" crashes.** Some code was compiled for a newer CPU
  than the one running it, nearly always because a `-m` or `-march` flag
  crept into `Makevars` or a personal `~/.R/Makevars`; remove any such flag.
* **`'highway-kernels.cpp' file not found` from `foreach_target.h`.**
  `PKG_CPPFLAGS` lacks `-I.` (section 4).
* **Undefined symbol `hwy::SupportedTargets()` or `hwy::Abort(...)` at load
  time.** `highway/impl.h` is not included anywhere: add `src/highway-impl.cpp`,
  or define `HWY_HEADER_ONLY` if you only use static dispatch.
* **"multiple definition of" or "duplicate symbol" `hwy::...` at link
  time.** `highway/impl.h` is included in more than one file; keep it in
  `highway-impl.cpp` only.
* **Only one target compiled.** If `HWY_DISABLED_TARGETS` leaves a single
  target, Highway turns `HWY_DYNAMIC_DISPATCH` into a direct call; this is
  correct behaviour, simply without dynamic dispatch.
* **Architectures without native SIMD in this package.** To keep the
  installed size within CRAN's limits, the back ends for POWER, s390x,
  RISC-V, LoongArch and WebAssembly are not bundled; there your code
  compiles and runs with Highway's portable `EMU128` target.
* **Apple clang and `bfloat16_t`.** Apple clang 21 crashes when compiling
  `LoadN` on 2-lane `bfloat16_t` vectors for the `NEON_BF16` target. Double
  and float code is unaffected; if you use `bfloat16_t`, consider adding
  `HWY_NEON_BF16` to `HWY_DISABLED_TARGETS` on macOS.
